query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings operating at high temperature under sliding, the primary mechanism governing wear resistance and microscopic deformation is the dynamic formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, partially amorphized tribolayer that promotes an inverse Hall-Petch behavior. This refined surface layer accommodates shear by activating multiple deformation pathways, thereby reducing wear and stabilizing deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-deposited FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate with a relatively coarse microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled pre-sliding thermal treatment (or thermal/processing step) designed to promote near-surface grain refinement, establishing conditions that favor rapid dynamic amorphization during sliding.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding conditions (e.g., operating temperatures where diffusion and dislocation mobility are elevated), where friction-induced heat and stress can further enhance the tribolayer formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, partially amorphous near-surface layer (tribolayer) that alters the effective grain boundary structure and dislocation pathways.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature sliding, the combined effects of thermal activation and mechanical stress cause the original coarse grains to dynamically refine into a nanocrystalline tribolayer. This refined layer reduces the local shear strength (via inverse Hall–Petch behavior) and redistributes deformation through activation of multiple slip systems, leading to lower wear and controlled microscopic deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, the thermally pre-treated coating will form a more pronounced ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer during sliding, resulting in decreased wear rates and reduced deleterious microscopic deformation (e.g., lower micro-cracking and reduced cavitation phenomena).
generation.baseline: A standard FeNiCrCoCu coating without the pre-sliding thermal treatment, exhibiting comparatively coarser grains and less efficient adaptive tribolayer formation under high-temperature sliding.
generation.boundary: These effects are predicted to hold at high operating temperatures during sliding. At lower temperatures or in static conditions (where the dynamic formation of the nanolayer is limited), the mechanism may not dominate wear behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While similar mechanisms have been observed in related HEA systems (e.g., inverse Hall-Petch behavior leading to ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayers in CoCrFeMnNi), it remains uncertain how the presence of Cu and the specific phase equilibria in FeNiCrCoCu will quantitatively affect the exact grain size thresholds and wear reduction in the high-temperature regime.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on identical substrates: one set with the controlled pre-sliding thermal treatment (designed to promote near-surface grain refinement) and one as a baseline. Conduct high-temperature sliding wear tests under identical load, speed, and temperature conditions. Post-test, use high-resolution microscopy (TEM/ STEM/ EBSD) to characterize the near-surface microstructure and quantify the extent of nanocrystalline tribolayer formation.
measurements: Quantitative wear rate (volume loss per unit sliding distance and load)
Grain size distribution and phase identification in the near-surface region (via TEM/EBSD)
Presence and thickness of any amorphous or ultra-nanocrystalline tribolayer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated coatings do not exhibit a significantly thinner wear track, lower wear rates, or demonstrably finer, adaptive tribolayers compared to the baseline, then the hypothesized mechanism—that dynamic nanocrystallization and partial amorphization govern the improved wear resistance—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
